n: Jonah was a real prophet from Galilee who served during the reign of Jeroboam II (around 790–750 BC). The Lord now gives him an unusual assignment.
God sends Jonah to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria — Israel’s brutal enemy — to warn it. God cares even about Israel’s enemies.

f.g: A major city, later the capital, of the Assyrian Empire, on the Tigris River in modern Iraq.

f.w: their wickedness is come up before me

n: Jonah runs the opposite direction — west toward Tarshish, perhaps in Spain, the far edge of the known world. Notice he keeps going “down”: down to Joppa, down into the ship.

f.g: A distant port, probably in Spain — about as far from Nineveh as one could go.
A port on Israel’s Mediterranean coast; modern Jaffa, near Tel Aviv.

f.w: from the presence of the LORD

n: The Lord hurls a great wind onto the sea. The storm is so violent that the ship is about to break apart. You cannot outrun God.

f.w: the LORD sent out a great wind
f.g: Literally “hurled” a wind — the same verb used later when the sailors hurl cargo and Jonah overboard.

n: The pagan sailors pray desperately, each to his own god, and throw cargo overboard. Meanwhile Jonah has gone down into the ship’s hold and is sound asleep.

f.w: cried every man unto his god
f.g: The crew came from many nations and religions.
A deep sleep — the same word used for Adam’s sleep in Genesis 2:21.

n: The captain wakes Jonah: “How can you sleep? Get up and pray to your God! Maybe He will save us.” A pagan has to urge the prophet to pray.
The sailors cast lots to find out who is to blame, and the lot falls on Jonah. The Lord directs even this.
They pepper Jonah with questions: What do you do? Where are you from? What people are you?

f.g: Business or mission — ironically, Jonah is fleeing his.

n: Jonah declares he is a Hebrew who worships the Lord, Creator of sea and land. The irony: he claims to fear the God he is running from — the very God who made the sea he is sailing on.

f.g: To fear means to revere or worship.

n: Now the sailors are terrified. Jonah had told them he was fleeing from the Lord, and they realize how serious that is.
With the storm worsening, they ask Jonah what they should do to calm the sea.

f.g: Was growing more and more stormy.

n: Jonah tells them to throw him overboard. He accepts responsibility — though he would still rather die than go to Nineveh.
The kind-hearted sailors try hard to row back to shore rather than sacrifice Jonah, but the sea grows even wilder.

f.g: Literally “dug” — rowed with all their strength.

n: Now the sailors pray to Jonah’s God, the Lord, asking not to be held guilty for his death. These foreigners show more reverence than the prophet.
They throw Jonah into the sea, and it immediately becomes calm.

f.w: the sea ceased from her raging

n: The sailors now fear the Lord deeply, offer sacrifice, and make vows. Even Jonah’s disobedience led others to God.

f.g: Promises to God, often to offer sacrifices later.

n: God “prepared” a great fish to swallow Jonah — not to punish but to rescue him. Jesus cited Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign of His own death and resurrection.

f.g: The Hebrew says “great fish,” not specifically a whale; Matthew’s Greek uses a word for “sea monster.”
